utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, have you completed your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I need another half an hour for examination, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Half an hour? Yes. Try for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. I will try to conclude as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, the period when the terrorism escalated in Kosovo in 1998 and until the end, at that time you were head of the Yugoslav mission at the UN?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, Kosovo as an internal issue of a sovereign state, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, how was that issue internationalised? How did it reach the Security Council's agenda?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosovo reached the Security Council's agenda through the Contact Group, which was established for Bosnia and Herzegovina, however in 1997 started looking into the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. We objected to that, however, the answer was that the Contact Group could look into and discuss any issue it wanted. As the practice of the Security Council was to get the views of the Contact Group prior to the issue being put on the agenda of the Security Council, all of these issues were discussed there first and then permanent members and later on also temporary members of the Security Council took into account and complied with the opinion of the Contact Group, which we opposed. We protested concerning that, however, they disregarded that protest of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you lodged protests, did you point out that that was a violation of the principle of the UN not to discuss internal issues of one state?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We expressed our opposition to that, but as I've already said, the Contact Group believed it was entitled to discuss about the internal issues of our country. And after that initial occasion, they simply introduced it into the regular practice of Security Council through the back door, and from then on it became a regular practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you as head of the Yugoslav mission at the UN received numerous documents about the crimes committed by the terrorist organisation called KLA against policemen, civilians, and so on throughout 1998 and 1999. Did you receive such information?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive that information on a -- I would say a rather regular basis. Based on the instructions we received from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, we would forward that information together with my supporting material to the Security Council and ask that that be registered as the UN documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that done?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever there was such an order, it was done in accordance with that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you also receive documentation of our government pertaining to the NATO aggression against our country?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And we applied the same procedure, because we would inevitably always receive instructions to forward that documentation to the Secretary-General and request that it be registered as the UN documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, in order to save time, I would like to point to you that in tab 28 - and you gentlemen as well - in tabs 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33 and 34. Therefore, in tab 27 [as interpreted], we have a document entitled "Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija and Albania." If you turn the page, if you turn the first page dated September 1998, you can see that the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs is the agency that issued it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's in binder 2. Tab 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what binder is this in; 1 or 2, tab 28? Is it tab 28 or tab 27?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28 up until 34. So tabs -- seven tabs containing documents. I assume that Mr. Jovanovic has the same copy as you do. I don't know if it's binder 1 or 2. It's not marked in my notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is marked as tab 1 in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In binder 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Binder 2 is not headed Terrorism. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's tab 30, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Tab 34 is Terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, and it contains the documents of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. I suppose that in order to be as rational as possible in our use of time, Mr. Robinson, we could cover all these documents now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, these documents of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, are these documents that you distributed in your capacity as the Yugoslav ambassador to the UN to other officials of the UN?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was sent to the Secretary-General, and in addition to that, we also send these documents to certain members of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following this, from 28 until tab 34, first we have NATO Crimes in Yugoslavia, documentary evidence, 24th of March to 24th of April. And then the next one is NATO Crimes in Yugoslavia, documentary evidence, 25th of April, 10th of June. Then we have the next one, Terrorist Acts of Albanian Terrorist Groups in Kosovo and Metohija, documents and evidence, 1st of January, 1998, to 10th of June, 1999, part 1. Then we have that same title in the following book, part 2. And then we have Crimes Committed by Albanian Terrorists in the Territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo since the 10th of June, 1999, documents and evidence, part 1. And then we have that same title part 2. So these are all documents containing facts, photographs. Therefore, this is the documentation issued by official agencies of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia sent to the UN and its officials via this witness who was Yugoslav ambassador to the UN. I ask that these seven documents be tendered into evidence. And let me just note that, as Mr. Kwon said, these documents were previously marked for identification. I referred to these documents during my various statements and opening statement, and this witness, through his official channels, forwarded these documents to various UN bodies and officials. Therefore, I ask that this be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me understand. These are documents that would have been prepared by government agencies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. These are official documents. You can see that it says Ministry of Foreign Affairs here. This ministry published these documents for these purposes precisely. And all of these documents were transferred to UN officials by this witness while he was ambassador there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So all information would have been collected by government agencies on behalf of the government.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by government agencies, by citizens in the field. All of these documents, photographs. I don't know whether photographs were taken by government agencies or perhaps by some teams who were in charge of that, however, you can see the documents, names of the people, photographs, events that were documented; everything else that accompanied these events. You can see that there are plenty of photographs here. All of the events are described as well. There are many documents attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the position about the production of these exhibits be reserved until I've asked a couple of questions about it? Unless you want to hear an argument now. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was really doing some of your work when I asked you those questions, because you really need to lay a better foundation than you have done so far for the admission of the documents. I've asked you how the information was collected. That's the kind of questions that you need to put to the witness. How they were transmitted to the witness, and then what he did with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I wanted to save the time. The witness is very well familiar with the contents of these documents. I can cover with him every book and it will take several hours. However, I wanted to be as efficient as possible, because these are documents issued by official government agencies. And this witness in his official capacity sent these documents to the UN officials; Secretary-General and other UN bodies. This is why I asked that they be exhibited. If you want me to cover all of these documents in their entirety, I'm prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. Just by asking three or four questions of the witness you can lay the foundation for their admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, how did you come to have these documents?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents were sent via diplomatic couriers or via mail. I don't think we used mail because it wasn't reliable, so they must have arrived via diplomatic couriers. Immediately upon receipt of these documents we would forward them to the United Nations and a number of officials and agencies in New York. Our aim was to inform the public, which was poorly informed about the events in Kosovo and Metohija, the public in the US, about the actual situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, every time you received some of these documents, did you make sure that you familiarised yourself with the contents of these documents?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I can't say that I studied every word of these documents. However, I went over them, compared them to the photographs that looked very shocking, and I could see that these documents are very concrete because they listed names, last names of the victims, as well as sites where these events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even before these documents arrived, did you receive through regular communication with the ministry from Belgrade information about the events as they were unfolding chronologically?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received that information as well, and we would always forward it to the president of the Security Council or Secretary-General, however, more often to the president of the Security Council, asking that it be distributed to other members of the Security Council because all of this had to do with the regular issues on the agenda of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These documents that you received after and the information contained in them, was it in accordance with what you learned later?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that they were in accordance, because we could compare that and the information that arrived subsequently.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, should we cover now each book individually?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's necessary, I think certainly for me, to know how these books were compiled and what the sources of the information in them were. It's not so much what you did with them that's the issue, it's how they were made up, so that we can see -- to help us to consider what value to place on them if they are to be admitted. Now, do you know how they were compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know specifically, but it was clear to me that they were collected on the basis of a series of statements and stories told by the victims and investigations on the spot by the competent authorities and a series of photographs taken on the spot by private individuals or anybody else who happened to be there or the judiciary, members of the court who took part in the investigation. So as I was in New York, I can't tell you what actually happened in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I thought was the position, Mr. Jovanovic. So you were effectively the postman delivering these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents and making sure they got proper attention at the New York end, but you had no responsibility for actually compiling the documents themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. But I wasn't only a postman either. I interpreted the information in my numerous meetings and encounters with colleagues, members of the Security Council, and the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were an ambassadorial postman. Would it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My only observations in light of the material that's been elicited by questions from His Honour Judge Bonomy is that in broadly similar documents, "As Seen, As Told" or "Under Orders," evidence was given directly to the Chamber by either the compiler or the person in charge of compilation of the book who was able to speak personally and in respect of the supervision of others as to the methodology of preparation and therefore as to its reliability, in one or both cases the authors having spoken of their methods of verifying the accuracy of the documents concerned, so that this document falls into a different category.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I intervene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As it's so often the right questions being asked and even this witness, who may have been a postman, but he looked at the material and would be able to recognise the documents. They're from public documents. They're autopsy reports, they're court investigative statements. It's actually better material than "As Seen, As Told" because it's the official documents within the FRY system that would have been put together as part of any crime scene analysis that has been compiled here to produce the evidence. So they largely come from Ministry of Justice reports or police reports, pathologist reports, and are based on I'm going to say government. I'm looking for the relevant state department's materials. And so in that context they are official documents that have been put together by some agency. It's a question of the right questions being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Mr. Milosevic just illustratively to take us through some of the information in the documents. Just say three or four so we can see what they are.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson. I shall be happy to do so. I'd just like to draw your attention to what Mr. Nice said a moment ago. This is far more important and much more valid evidence than the book "As Seen, As Heard" [as interpreted] written by different authors. These are official documents by the authorities who were in charge of conducting investigations and establishing what had happened in the field, that is to say the organs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia. And by way of an example, here we have one. Take a look at the first book, NATO Crimes in Yugoslavia, for instance, documentary evidence, 21st of March to the 24th -- or, rather, 24th of March to April 1999, and if you look at page, for instance, page 32. It follows the photographs, the set of photographs. Or, for example, after the first set of photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 32.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can take a look at page 21. After the first set of photographs. I don't know if you have the photographs. You can see a human hand, a severed head of a man who was killed. On page 21 you can see that this is an official document. It says the Republic of Serbia, Ministry of the Interior, Secretariat of the Interior in Djakovica, the dispatch number is 2583/99, the date is the 14th of April, 1999, Djakovica. Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia is the addressee. Criminal police, HQ, police HQ, Operations Centre. Well, I can read it out in English to make it easier on the interpreters. It says: "Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, Criminal Police Headquarters, Police Headquarters, [In English] Operations Centre Belgrade, Ministry of the Interior Headquarters Pristina." [Interpretation] And then it says, "On the 14th of April, 1999, between 1.30 p.m. and 3.30 p.m., [In English] the criminal NATO forces committed an air assault on a column of refugees --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, regardless of the language. Thank you. A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, you're getting carried away. You're getting excited, and you're going too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Anyway, this is an official letter naming the people identified on the spot, and it says: "Martin Hasanaj, Lek Hasanaj, Salji Djokaj, Skendi Djokaj," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic. Let's move to another one. I have seen this one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. It was signed by the superintendent Colonel Milan Kovacevic, secretariat superintendent. So this is an official letter preceded by photographs. And then if you turn the page, you will see the same thing. To the Ministry of the Interior, from Pristina, et cetera, et cetera, and an explanation. The document was signed this time by Colonel Milovan Kovacevic. And the following document on page 25 was signed by Lieutenant Colonel Milan Stanojevic, and it says what happened in the village of Madanaj. 19 persons were killed, six persons wounded. And then he goes on to explain what happened near the village of Meja, the Terzijski bridge, the village of Meja, Terzijski bridge, and the village of Gradis. Then page 26, a report on the on-site forensic technical investigation, signed by forensic technicians Veselin Vesovic, Ljubisa Djordjevic, Nebojsa Vuksanovic, Nebojsa Avramovic, and then an explanation of what happened there, and this is followed by a set of photographs pertaining to all of that. I happened to open the page at page 32, the document at page 32, and there, too, you can see what was going on. NATO strike on the Prizren-Djakovica road. It says enclosure on-site inspection, topographic map, photographic and technical documentation of the site, forensic technical report, and so on and so forth. Then you have some maps. And if you turn the page there to page 34, once again a report. The signatures. So we're dealing here with these. A series of photographs next. Signatures again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you look at the preface, the preface was written by minister of foreign affairs, and it says that it was --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "The aim of this book is to present to the international public the evidence about crimes." So having read that, I think Mr. Jovanovic can explain the purpose of this book and the way of compilation, since you are in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, even though you were in New York.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic wasn't the foreign minister. He was the head of the Yugoslav mission to the United Nations. Before that he was the foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The foreign minister was also a man named Jovanovic but his name was Zivadin Jovanovic and he wrote the preface with the intention of informing the world public who was overly bombed and supersaturated with one-sided presentations of the NATO aggression and the development of events over there. So they wanted to inform the world public with the specific concrete findings of the competent authorities so that they could gain a true picture of what was happening in Yugoslavia as the result of the NATO bombing. And that preface of his is something that is logical to my mind because it is a book compiled by the Foreign Ministry, and he as minister said a few words by way of explanation what it was all about in the preface.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you indicated earlier that you had some questions to ask in relation to the admission of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Most of them have effectively -- most of them have effectively been raised by His Honour Judge Bonomy, and it seems to me the conclusion that one could draw is that this witness has no firsthand knowledge of the contents and was not involved directly in the preparation and did not supervise the preparation of the book. That makes it different from "As Seen, As Told" or from "Under Orders." It's also, of course, different in that the participants in the compilation of the book may be thought to have been those with an interest and not those who were disinterested in the way that the contributors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All of that goes to weight. That's why I asked him earlier -- remember I asked him if it was collected by government servants of different agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the points I would have sought to have pressed home through cross-examination. I don't desire to take more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We could mark it for identity, and Mr. Milosevic, and it would be then in your interest to bring a witness who could speak to the manner of compilation so that we would be able to attach more weight to it than we can now. Because it wasn't compiled by the ambassador or under his supervision. It was compiled under the supervision, no doubt, of somebody working in the Ministry of the Interior. So if you were to bring that witness from the Ministry of the Interior who supervised the compilation, it would enhance the weight that the Chamber would be able to attach to the information and would meet some of the arguments raised by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues] ... and so on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before you make a ruling, open page 56, for example, please. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which volume? Which volume?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same volume. I'm taking this as an example. Turn to page 56. Be so good as to turn to page 56, please. I don't know which official of the ministry you need to give weight to this. This provides -- this sets out the investigation report "[In English] Made on April 6, 1999, by Investigative Judge of the Aleksinac Municipal Court relating to the bombing of Aleksinac by NATO war planes on April 5, 1999, which caused the death of several persons, serious and minor injuries of several persons, and extensive material damage." [Interpretation] And then it says here present on behalf of the Court [In English] Court Clerk, President of the Court, District Attorney's office, Forensic Technician, Expert Consultants. [Interpretation] And so and so forth. And then you have description of the scene. And it goes on to explain which houses were targeted, who the proprietors of the houses were, which streets, the street numbers of the houses, and a whole page devoted to the figures, the number of houses, the owners who were hit, the houses who were hit. So these are documents, authentic documents, authentic reports by the court organs. I assume you really don't need an official from the ministry to explain any of this, how this information was gathered. These are official facts and figures compiled by the courts, the police, the state organs of Yugoslavia, and I can just make -- add this: Each of these documents, and there are thousands of them in these books, can be a separate exhibit in itself and proof in itself. If you want me to go through them one by one and turn them all into exhibits, I'll be happy to do so, it won't be difficult for me. For example, if you look at the Aleksinac report for which Mr. Nice said that the barracks were targeted whereas here we can see all the houses, the residential apartment buildings in the centre of Aleksinac were targeted and destroyed should be a separate subject. I don't -- I didn't think that weight was given by the form it was packed up in. But if you would like, I would turn all these books into thousands of exhibits and then you can see for yourselves. But if you want to reject court documents of what actually happened, then go ahead and do so, but then that speaks of something else, doesn't it, that we're not talking about the Ministry of Foreign Affairs here. These are documents, court documents and other documents of state organs with documents provided and attached with the findings attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, as you said, there are thousands and hundreds of documents here. Are they all official documents, documents of ministry? How can you verify that? There's so many.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I'm going to turn them into 1.000 exhibits and I'm going to verify all of them. That's no problem whatsoever, because in the book they were published. I mean, the contents of these documents. We're going to take the photocopies of these documents, we're going to take the findings of experts, of forensic experts, of court authorities, and we're going to exhibit all of them. If you want me to do it that way, I'm going to do it that way. No problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please try to understand at least my concern about the way in which this is being presented. This witness has told us all he obviously can about these documents, and that's fine, because it's important to demonstrate that they got to the United Nations and they were a representation of a case being made on behalf of your country to the United Nations. But there's a large volume of material here, and it's your job to present it in a form which will enable us to give it the maximum weight. This is obviously important material, if you can justify presenting it in a proper way. Now, what I need to know is how it was compiled. Because a lot of it is summaries of events. They're not all official documents. Perhaps the majority are, I don't know, but it's obvious they're not all official documents. So we need to know how this exercise was carried out and how in general we should approach our consideration of it. And all that needs is a witness from one of the ministries who was responsible for compiling this or supervising its compilation to come and tell us about it. At the moment, all that's happening is time is being wasted in relation to the evidence of an important witness who really can't add anything on this particular material. So there will be a way of doing it. It could even be done in writing. Either that or by a statement subject to cross-examination or something of that nature. There are many ways of introducing this material in the right form without taking up the time of witnesses who can't really speak to it. And I need to be addressed, before I'm prepared to accept that it should be admitted, to hear evidence about the way in which it was put together.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are deliberating, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you take a look at tab 30, tab 30, page 259. On the left side, on page 258, it says that it's a report on ballistic expert examination, but on page -- from page 209 [sic], there are a number of paragraphs which summarise Albanian terrorist attacks. Is it a summary done by whom or whether they are official documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just have a look, from 209.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Oh, 259. Yes, 259. All right. 259, then. Oh, the numbers are 665, 666, 667. Events that were registered by the official authorities. But there's something wrong. It cannot start from 665. And then further on -- then 664 must have been the previous event. These are events that were registered by the authorities in charge. This is not information from the newspaper. They are supported by documents that are held by the competent agencies. So these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. are not summaries, these are descriptions of specific events. Look at 665: "In the night of the 17th and 18th of November, 1998, Albanian terrorists fired several shots from automatic weapons towards the garage and repair service in Pec, property of Ali Berisha, born in 1934, hitting the facility with 22 bullets."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not clear from the document itself who compiled this paragraph, from where. So you can call a witness who is able to answer these kind of questions, which no doubt will strengthen your case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And probably one witness could cover all the binders by telling us how this job was done. Otherwise, we're left to fish around and try to -- and indeed we would be required to speculate to some extent, which is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I find this very useful what you've been saying now, because it's obvious that importance is not being attached to substance. It is the form that counts, to give it an acceptable form. Mr. Kwon, you opened this book now, Terrorist Acts by Albanian Terrorists and Terrorist Groups in Kosovo and Metohija, documents in evidence from the 1st of January, 1998 to the 10th of June, 1999. All of this information is supplied by official authorities. Then I also opened the first book about NATO crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the passage to which Judge Kwon refers, there is nothing there to say how it was compiled. You cannot yourself give evidence. I've told you that before. There's absolutely nothing on that page to show where that information came from, and that's the point that Judge Kwon is making, and Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well. You're going to get all of these books, all of these documents as a separate exhibit with court reports. There's going to be several thousand of them, and then we're going to look at them, because you yourselves insist on it. I assume that you're going to give me sufficient time for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you wish to be silly, that's your business, but don't waste the time of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Behaviour like a spoiled child is quite inappropriate in a forum such as this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are discussing an important matter of the weight that we will be able to attach to these thousands of pages, and the point is that we will be able to attach little weight to it if we don't know how it was compiled. So there's no point behaving in this silly fashion. I will not tolerate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think court-assigned counsel or the associate can assist you in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll mark these documents for identification, and the Court advises Mr. Milosevic to produce a witness who can give credible testimony as to how the information in these documents was compiled. Do you have any further questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have more questions, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, in paragraph 96 of the Kosovo document, it says -- or, rather, there is reference made to Resolution 1160 and then 1199 of the Security Council. The other ones are not mentioned. I'm going to read part of this paragraph out to you. It says: "In response to the intensifying conflict, the United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 1160 in March 1998 'condemning the use of excessive force by Serbian police forces against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo,' and imposed an arms embargo on the FRY. Six months later, the UN Security Council passed Resolution 1199 (1998) which stated that 'the deterioration of the situation in Kosovo, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, constitutes a threat to peace and security in the region.' The Security Council demanded that all parties cease hostilities and that 'security forces used for civilian repression' be withdrawn." So, Security Council Resolutions about Kosovo and Metohija, because this paragraph doesn't show that, do they refer to terrorist activities? Do they condemn them? You were there then, you followed these events. You received all these Resolutions. Tell us as briefly as possible in response to my question whether Security Council Resolutions about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, do they mention terrorist activities and do they condemn them?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the situation in Kosovo was discussed and during the NATO aggression, there was a total of four Security Council Resolutions. In all of them, there is explicit condemnation of terrorist acts and terrorism, or they call upon the Albanian leaders to do their best to have such activities stopped. In addition to these Security Council Resolutions, in one of the Resolutions of the General Assembly terrorist activities were also condemned, also, there were some reports of the Secretary-General of the UN that were submitted to the Security Council that indicated terrorist activities of the KLA in Kosovo vis-a-vis civilians, both Albanians and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, since you were in New York then and since you followed all the reactions, was the KLA qualified as a terrorist organisation; and if so, by who?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA was first placed on the State Department list as a terrorist organisation. In all fairness, at that time it was not known as the KLA, but the terrorist groups that were operating at the time, much less then than later on, were considered to be terrorist groups. This was in 1997. In 1998, they were treated as a terrorist group. And I think that Ambassador Gelbard, if I remember his name correctly, was the one who sometime in February that year called the KLA a terrorist group beyond any doubt. Later on, this terrorist group or organisation grew into the so-called Freedom Fighters, and during the NATO aggression they became the infantry of NATO in Kosovo and Metohija and in Albania from where they carried out incursions into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whose perception was this that the terrorist organisation of the KLA was -- became Freedom Fighters?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was under the influence of the US government primarily and NATO. They were representing this terrorist group as the so-called protectors of the Albanian people that were threatened, as was said, and then they were accepted as Freedom Fighters. I omitted to mention that Ambassador Richard Holbrooke established the first contact with them. I think this was in 1998 when he visited one of their bases, crossed his legs, sat and talked to them and practically legalised them in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you're probably giving some of the answers that I wanted, but you said that the KLA became the infantry of NATO. Could you explain that? How did they become the infantry of NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Soldiers of the UCK frequently crossed from Kosovo to the territory of Albania and vice versa. And at the time when the bombing was the fiercest in an area called Kosara, which is on our territory, these UCK units attacked numerously Yugoslav border, across the border, and that was followed by a synchronised NATO action which targeted our soldiers who had left their shelters in order to protect the borders from armed attacks. There are many statements in the press about that, and this is not something that NATO kept quiet either. On the other hand, the UCK soldiers were exposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The sequence of KLA attacks followed by NATO bombing suggested that there was some collaboration between NATO and the KLA. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what is stated by some leaders of the UCK or KLA, as it is called. Later on, in their books they wrote that the goal was to get Yugoslav Serb soldiers out to a clear terrain where they would be easily targeted by NATO planes. This is what was publicly stated. A lot of our soldiers were killed in the process of that action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is the basis, that is the sole basis for your conclusion that there was collaboration, the sequence of KLA attacks followed by NATO bombing. I mean, do you have any other evidence to support what is obviously your thesis that there was some collaboration between NATO and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several reports in Western media. This is not something that was kept silent, kept quiet. President Clinton, in honour of what he did for Albanians and Kosovo, had a main square in Pristina named after him, and also several other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A monument was built in his honour as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you were in New York at the time, so please tell us, did NATO receive any kind of approval, indirect approval even, for its aggression against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't even try to get an approval because they knew that one -- at least one of the members of Security Council would veto it. This is why they proceeded into the action without applying to the Security Council at all. Leaders of NATO countries later on tried to justify this by saying that in previous Resolutions of the Security Council, Chapter VII had been mentioned. However, these were very unconvincing arguments, analyses that could not be supported by the Charter or other documents and that were really not taken seriously by anyone, even in Western countries. In a series of reports issued by -- or statements given by President Clinton and various other NATO and Western leaders, they always availed themselves of some new arguments. They never insisted on the same arguments. So that initial thesis that justified this action was not acceptable even to those who advocated it initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, based on the assessment, evaluations of foreign diplomats that you came across at the UN, please tell us whether the authority of the UN was destroyed as a result of this NATO action.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly it was. When I gave a speech at the UN and when I compared this case to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're not concerned, as I think Your Honour Judge Robinson said yesterday, with the international community's behaviour and response, and as I've said on several earlier occasions, the accused is using his opportunity to ask questions as a way of advancing political positions and propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm asking the witness about a speech he gave at the Security Council. Therefore, this is not an academic issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that you asked is whether the authority of the UN was destroyed as a result of this NATO action, and that is totally an irrelevant matter. So move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well, Mr. Robinson. The crimes of NATO are not relevant for you. This is just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've cut you off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, what did you say in your speech given before the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed them that on the 24th, on such-and-such time, an aggression against Yugoslavia had commenced, that it had no basis. It was not based on anything that was written in the Charter of the UN and that the Security Council was the only one that could authorise the use of force against another UN member state. I gave figures about casualties, and I warned that this was a heavy blow to the UN because an armed action was being carried out against a UN member state without the approval of the Security Council, which is the only body authorised to authorise such use of force. And then I said that if such an action is being allowed, then we should ask ourselves who is going to be the next target. I reminded them of the sad fate of the League of Nations and the case of Italy and the then Abyssinia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's irrelevant. Move on to an issue that's relevant. And you should now be concluding your examination-in-chief. This witness has been here from Monday. We are now at Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please take a look at tab 17.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. Robinson, that you will not decline my request to have this exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In which binder?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, tab 17. I have just one single binder. Therefore, I can't tell you whether it's binder 1 or 2 in your document. However, it's tab 17. This is a document providing the definition of aggression. And in the footnote it says: "Official Records of the General Assembly, the 29th session..." Therefore, this is an official text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tab 17?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. And this is the document that brings the definition of aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, if you wish, you could call me as a witness. I was involved in the negotiations that produced that definition in 1974. But do you need this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I need you to testify? I suppose that you've already testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of aggression.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is necessary to have it introduced into evidence, because this institution of yours is constantly declaring itself not to have jurisdiction over the crimes committed by Western powers in the territory of Yugoslavia so you should change the name of the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I make some observations. I think the accused is going far too far. We divide up the two things that have happened recently. Were it to be relevant for the Chamber to consider the definition of aggression, that would be a public document that wouldn't be to be produced in the course of these proceedings. It would simply be available. Second, the accused's questioning and his attitude to the Court is a matter that the Court, in our respectful submission, could view very seriously. Freedom of expression granted to an accused representing himself is one thing; to be contemptuous of the Court is entirely something else. Now, we recognise that this accused has no respect for the Court - he's made that clear - and may be untroubled by any sanctions of a conventional kind that the Court could impose on him, but we also recognise that this accused now understands that the Court has the ability to curtail the amount of time in which he may present his case, and it would be our submission that the Chamber could start the process of considering docking time, reducing time when the accused behaves as offensively to the Chamber as he has started to do today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll not admit this. Every student in law, international law, knows about the definition of aggression. It is something that you can refer to in your closing address, if you wish. If you do not have any more questions, I will terminate your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have several more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not several more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you continue to ask questions that are not relevant, I'm going to terminate your examination-in-chief, so bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. I suppose that it is relevant what is stated in count 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will read it out, Mr. Jovanovic, the very end of this paragraph. It pertains to Rambouillet, and the last sentence goes as follows: "Despite intensive negotiations over several weeks, the peace talks collapsed in mid-March 1999." Are you familiar with these intensive negotiations which collapsed in mid-March 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with them based on my following of the Rambouillet peace process while I was in New York and based on the reports we regularly received from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Based on that, I know that there were in fact no negotiations at all, rather, mediating activity on behalf of members of the Contact Group, Ambassador Hill, and so on. And there were no contacts between the representatives of the UCK and our delegation. No agreement was reached on that score. Just one agreement was reached, and that was the agreement reached by representatives of non-Albanian ethnic communities in Kosovo and our government. Everything else cannot be called an agreement but, rather, some contacts and documents signed by members, representatives of the UCK and representatives of the Contact Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You as an experienced diplomat, what do you say about the statement here that the peace negotiations collapsed in mid-March 1999? If the peace negotiations collapsed, then how come these agreements were reached?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I tried to explain. They collapsed because no agreement was reached between main sides, main parties invited to negotiations. The only agreement that was reached, this so-called interim agreement on peace and self-government in Kosovo is the agreement signed by the representatives of the Albanian side. And this agreement was witnessed by several members of the Contact Group. However, this is not an agreement either in political or legal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, just one more question to you. You have vast experience. You spent many years in foreign service. So please tell us, do you know something about the International Crisis Group? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the International Crisis Group? Very briefly, please, because we're about to finish.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know has to do with us, Kosovo and our region. This group in that respect was and remained quite active, and it took positions which were practically always against the interests of Serbia and Yugoslavia and favoured the idea of independent Kosovo and Metohija, or at least its breaking away from Serbia and Yugoslavia. They mentioned or brought up several arguments in favour of that, which is not surprising, because the founder of that group, Mr. Morton Abramowitz who, inter alia, was an advisor and then -- advisor to the Albanian leaders in Rambouillet, showed bias and prejudice in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, we'll just take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I was wondering if I might just have two minutes of Your Honours' time after the witness has withdrawn. Nothing to do with the substance of his evidence but it may be helpful if I explain something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you may leave now. We're going to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just this: Recently we've seen, of course, the calculation of time that's passed so far where we, in accommodation with procedural matters, exceeded the two-thirds period of time. We've also now received a list of witnesses from the accused. That causes me considerable concern for the following reason: By my calculation and assuming we're able to keep to the two-thirds limit, the list of witnesses would take us I think to June, or thereabouts. That's my calculation. And yet, although there are some crossover witnesses, he's still dealing with Kosovo. I am concerned for the following reason that I set out in earlier argument and indeed in writing, that in the Prosecution's case, when given time limits, the accused habitually asked questions that seemed not to be the point until towards the end of the allotted time and then would raise clearly relevant matters, almost compelling the Chamber to grant him an extension of the time limit. I've expressed the concern that he may take the same attitude generally in relation to the conduct of his defence. With that in mind, I'm as determined as I can be to accomplish cross-examination briefly. Thus, for example, the latest proposal that I've put in place for this witness, to make documents available to the witness ahead of cross-examination, which I hope - we'll have to see - may speed the process. Inevitably with witnesses like this where we can't approach them surgically, we don't have a detailed statement, if we are to deal with all the evidence they give coming completely as a surprise for the most part and the case that we have to put, the two-thirds time limit would not be possible. I'm going to be selective. Again I've heralded this before, and necessarily so, with this witness and indeed with all witnesses, and I would simply ask the Chamber's understanding of that, where I seek to put in exhibits comparatively swiftly and recognising the fact that I will not be able to put all of my case to such a witness as this as the Rules require me to do. I'll be selective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's a matter for you, Mr. Nice. The Chamber is concerned about the use of time, and it's a matter which we have under consideration, and we'll be issuing an order shortly in relation to the matters that are relevant to that issue. But we are very concerned about the use of time. We will take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm going to ask you no questions about the content or substance of the white books, but we've seen the very detailed way in which they are prepared with resources you've described. Can you tell me, please, is there a similar document of research into the killing and expulsion of Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there is but they're not documents that came to me, nor did I further those documents to anybody else. Those documents were written by the people and the organisations which were mostly favourably disposed towards the Albanians and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short. Your government's resources were deployed, as we can see, to prepare a detailed analysis of what it was said was done against them. You all knew of the allegations made about expulsion and killing of Kosovo Albanians, who Serbia regards, as you will tell us, equal citizens with Serbs. Can you tell us, please, why there was no similar analysis prepared in respect to the killings and expulsions?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the white books there are a lot of names of Albanians and other non-Serbs who were the victims of different terrorist action in Kosovo and Metohija. So this isn't only the protection of Serbian victims but all the victims of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Yugoslav authorities were able to do so more and better than others because they were on the spot, and they had access to firsthand information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Can you just help us so that we can research it. Which book are we going to find the evidence of the killing of the Kosovo Albanians, which of the white books are we going to find evidence of the killing of Kosovo Albanians by Serb forces, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the killing of Kosovo Albanians by the terrorist organisation the KLA, and their names can be found there. Now, as far as the killing of Albanians by the police or army, they were killed in the fighting, in battle, and they were members of the KLA mostly. If there were civilian casualties in those conflicts anywhere, then that was regrettable, but it was not the aim of the operation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question on this topic, broad topic. Serbia has known since the late summer of 1995 of allegations about Srebrenica. Has it ever used its resources to prepare a report like the report in the white book dealing with the deaths of all those people in Srebrenica? Has it? And if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know that from the 4th of August, 1994, a cease-fire -- or, rather, a cessation to all economic and other relationships with Republika Srpska were set into motion, and so an insight into what happened there was very limited and small. So the fact -- this fact and this situation went on to the Dayton process up until the time when the leadership of Republika Srpska accepted that President Milosevic should speak on behalf of all of them at Dayton. Up until then, access to information and the possibility of influencing the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at all was for us very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what if any inquiry of the scale of the white book has been done for Srebrenica? None?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that because I wasn't in the country at the time. I was in New York. And on the other hand --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, is that a serious answer? You in New York dealing on a daily basis with allegations made about the former Yugoslavia, about Serbia, about Montenegro, you wouldn't know, you couldn't know whether a proper inquiry into Srebrenica had been conducted?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica is on the territory of another state. That's where it's located. And that territory was placed under some kind of protectorate after the Dayton agreement. And international armed forces came in, and they continued to be in authority there, in charge of analysing and investigating and managing that state. We didn't have any organs ourselves or the possibility of inspecting and analysing anything and arriving at evidence in that country on the basis of which we would be able to compile a book later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you did know that no such book had ever been made.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard about it. Perhaps it was made, but I never heard of one being in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope you had an opportunity since yesterday to look at some of the documents, or indeed all of the documents, provided to you in the files. Have you been able to do that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that yesterday I agreed to take on those documents, believing them to be few in number. However, I was given two large books like two Bibles, and it is impossible for one man to even leaf through them let alone read through them in such a short space of time. But despite that, I did do my best to become acquainted with their contents, and I noticed that there were a lot of records and minutes from the meetings of -- and sessions devoted to the coordination of foreign policy. The document is a secret one, and I personally am not prepared to discuss it until I have been lifted from keeping the -- the ban from keeping state secrets is lifted, until it was waived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was an observation you made almost immediately yesterday when you were confronted with the possibility of being asked to look at documents. Was that an answer you came prepared to give?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because yesterday's answer was to the Honourable President of the Trial Chamber, and I asked whether there were any state secrets in the document. I was assured that there were not. But when I looked at the text I saw that a considerable portion of the text were minutes or records from meetings of the Council for Coordinating Foreign Policy, which in other words, were documents of high state sensitivity, top secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These documents, Mr. Jovanovic, I must tell you have been provided without complaint by the government for use in these proceedings without any protective measures. I'm going to ask you questions about passages of those documents, and I'm going to ask you to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is an extraordinary proposition that this witness should now claim some limitation on giving evidence without having given advance notice, but we'll see how we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I come to those documents, Mr. Jovanovic, just this: There are about four topics, or three topics, and that's all I want to deal with with you. The first topic is the authority of the accused. The second topic is crimes or apparent crimes that were committed and the knowledge that was gained by you and by the accused of those crimes. The third topic is this, and I'll put it in the form of a question: It's right, as all these documents show, that throughout the period of negotiation and throughout the wars a prevailing ambition of all of you, the accused and you and other Serbs, was to achieve, in the end, a state where all Serbs could live together; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is completely incorrect, an incorrect approach, an incorrect thesis, and more even incorrect conclusion. Why? Because from the beginning we made efforts to preserve Yugoslavia, the kind of Yugoslavia that existed before the crisis. And when the crisis came about, we did our best to preserve at least those parts of the republic that had not come out in favour of independence. So this was an ongoing continuous process. And when they came out in favour of independence, that is to say Macedonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, when they gained international recognition, even before that and in the declaration adopted together with the constitution, we expressly stated that we had no territorial pretensions and claims on those territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, I've described this for the purposes -- using a neutral term. I'm not going to use "Greater Serbia" for the moment or "All Serbs in one state." I'm saying this was a prevailing ambition. In light of your answer, please tell me this: Did you personally, genuinely, seek for a multi-ethnic arrangement regardless of any domination by or co-existence with Serbs? Is that what you sought personally?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Bosnia-Herzegovina or the whole of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The whole of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our position was one of principle and firmly based on the constitution and its provisions and the free determination of all the nations that formed the first country, which was the country of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. So what was important for us was that this common state was the best for all, because all of us were there together, and all of us were great. When they started leaving, they became small and depended on others and faced a series of problems that this brought with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Given that the former Yugoslavia was going to disintegrate, did you have any personal desire to see a migration of ethnicities back to their mother countries so that you could have ethnically pure or ethnically dominated states? Did you, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not have desired that, even if people thought so, because Serbia itself was multi-ethnic. And after the break-up of Yugoslavia, it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is the sole republic that remained multi-ethnic to the end. And our sole aim was to preserve that state because it suited everybody best and was best able to solve the problem of having all people live in one state and not in a number of separate states. This is a natural position, a very humane one, so it cannot be challenged, and people can't say that we had ambitions at appropriating anything or forcing anybody to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, files provided to the Chamber and the witness and the accused yesterday have the same tab numbering system. The difference being that, of course, in the witness's, and the accused's indeed volumes, existing exhibits were included whereas it was only additional or new potential exhibits that were included in Your Honours' binders. So when I refer to, for example, tab 15, as I now do, it's a document not in your volumes. It's an existing exhibit, and I'm going to ask the witness, please, if he would be so good, as he may have looked at these documents and become familiar with them, to take the volume of his documents and go to tab 15, at page 89. I'd ask Mr. Nort, the usher, please, to display what is page 92 and then 93 on the overhead projector. This is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the shorthand notes for the Council for Harmonisation held on the 9th of January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there copies for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we discussed this in advance, and it seemed preferable, given the volume of material and given that of course the Chamber may have been working on its own versions of these documents, simply to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, what we're looking at here, Mr. Jovanovic, is the shorthand notes from something called the Council for Reconciliation on the Stands of State Policies. That's the way it's described. On the 9th of January. I needn't take you to cover page although we can see that, apart from yourself, it was presided over by Dobrica Cosic, the accused was present, as was Mr. Bulatovic, Mr. Djukanovic, Mr. Krajisnik, General Mladic, and others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should first like to address the Honourable Trial Chamber and remind them that these documents are of a very sensitive nature, and that I have not received a waiver from disclosing state secrets. If I was able to receive guarantees from the Trial Chamber that I would not be persecuted by -- prosecuted by my government, I could answer and respond to them, but I'm afraid that someone in my government might criticise me for responding or that I might be legally prosecuted for doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just remind us of the history behind this exhibit. It was exhibited --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The history behind this exhibit is that it was -- this particular one was provided voluntarily in answer to a request by the state, Serbia and Montenegro, without any suggestion of restriction on its use. And further, just to deal with the witness's observation, waivers are required for state and military secret, and this document is in fact headed "Strictly confidential." But even if there were any argument about there being state and military secret contained within it, that is clearly waived by the provision. Serbia and Montenegro knew perfectly well that these documents were for public use. Indeed, nothing could have been clearer because they took a slightly different view in relation to another series of documents and indeed have obtained rulings from the Chamber which reflect their limited concern, which was a concern of a state nature. It's never been suggested that individuals can't be allowed to speak about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Through which witness was this tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Lilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lilic. He had a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, he had a waiver. He was the first one with a waiver. He produced them, but he didn't discuss them. We looked at one passage of one of them with him, and the reason he didn't discuss them was all to do with want of time. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he had a waiver in respect of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- which would have included this one. Which would have included this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Waivers, of course, go to the individual, and the point that arose during the Prosecution case, if I can say this to assist the Trial Chamber, as this developed and Lilic became a witness, it was clear that he would be revealing matters that would otherwise be considered in terms of a government to be confidential state secrets. And to avoid any personal issue, great steps were taken to enable him to testify on such matters but with a waiver that was personal to him. The waiver, of course, doesn't go in relation to the use of the document. The waiver relates to the individual. And that should be something that is considered in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question then is whether there is anything in the document which would expose the witness to criminal charges and in respect of which a waiver would be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We won't know that until we get to a position where such an issue arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How could that issue possibly arise in relation to a document that was willingly released by the government of the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The document may be released without condition, but if the answers of the witness refer to matters outside the document as a result of the question, then of course there may be an area there that would be properly categorised as state secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that issue has got nothing to do with the document. That's a broader issue about whether the witness should have got a waiver before coming to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's right. That's why I'm raising it, so that the Court is aware, so to speak, of the full issue. Mr. Nice has addressed you in relation to the document, but the issue that also has to be considered is the position of the individual. And I raise this having been involved with these matters myself some months ago in relation to the production of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just make a point? This is a fully public document. People have had access to this document and been able to print it publicly, if they had wanted to, for months or it may be years. And of course -- my learned friend overstates it in his analysis of sensitivity in any event. It's only state and military secrets, I think, that are covered in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a public document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a public document; it is by virtue of being in this trial because publicly filed documents can be obtained by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we have attended to the concern that you have expressed, but in our view nothing arises in this document that would expose you to the danger you have identified, so answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Mr. Nort has the bottom of page 92 on the overhead projector, we see a contribution at the foot of that page, please, Mr. Nort, further up - thank you - from yourself. And you say this: "As far as the name is concerned, despite the resistance they've been offering against the state, I have the feeling that that possibility has not been laid out. I think we should insist in Geneva that everybody has the right to call himself by the name that suits him," this is for context, Mr. Jovanovic, "unless we cannot all be called confederal units, which would be the maximum. All the more so if it is completed by guarantees that we're going to give them concerning human rights. We must clearly, comprehensively and generously guarantee them that the enclaves within the provinces, that is to say within the confederal unit, would be fully protected and that the refugees would have the right to turn and be compensated for the destroyed property, et cetera." Thus far very good sentiments. But I want you now to read on what you said: "It will not work out because the natural migration towards the mother country would follow. Nobody has ever paid the war reparation anywhere, so I'm sure it will not happen here either. However, we have to make the comprehensive and generous gesture. Therefore, we must give a guarantee at the humanitarian aspect. We must guarantee that the non-existential creation called Bosnia would be held in such non-existential condition for many years. That should divert fears that the creation of Greater Serbia is ahead." What you're revealing there is that what you say in public is one thing, and it doesn't interfere with your underlying ambition that states should be joined up -- Serb states should be joined up in due course. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to repeat what I said to the President of the Honourable Trial Chamber. I was given assurances that I would not have to face any unpleasantness when I went back to my country, but I did not receive personal permission to comment documents of top state importance. Mr. Lilic received a waiver himself personally. I have not. I honour this Trial Chamber very much and your assurances, but I don't know whether they will be sufficient for my government to let me say what you would like to have me respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But there is nothing in the answer that you could give to this question that could expose you to any danger. It's really a straightforward question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is true, and I don't mind answering, but this is a question on the -- based on a document which is a state secret. It was provided to the Court because the Court asked for it. But had I been told beforehand that I would be discussing this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very aware of the consumption of time. I've made my position clear. I'm giving this witness the chance to comment on matters that go directly to his credit. If he chooses not to do so, I'm going to move on because I see the clock ticking. He doesn't want to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to your tab 16, Mr. Jovanovic, and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not afraid of answering. I can answer you, but I wanted to give that caution. I don't want to have any repercussions when I come home. I'm not sure they'll turn a blind eye to it. And I see no difference between what was said here and what we strove for, because this was preparation for negotiations and discussions in Geneva, as far as I understand it. I haven't been able to read the whole text, just the portion read out by you. And in Geneva, they will be discussing different types of organisation for the three communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina stemming from the confederal one and down to the cantonal ones. And we're discussing what could be the maximum aim of the Bosnian Serbs. And of course those who always opted for remaining in a joint state adhered to the maximum goal; that is to say that Bosnia and Herzegovina should become a confederal state. So we reviewed this question in different ways. We looked into the ways and means, and we wanted to quell them and tell them they would not be separated from a joint state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, that's a long answer but what I directed your attention to was the reference to natural migration, to no one paying for war reparation, having to make a gesture and guaranteeing the non-existential creation called Bosnia for years to avoid people worrying about Greater Serbia. My suggestion to you is that that reveals what your real ambition was. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right, not at all right, because it was contrary to what was said. It says here that we should insist upon the humanitarian aspect and allow people freely to decide where they're going to live. So not to quell them but to allay their fears. And as this Greater Serbia seems to be the bogeyman which was proliferated and fear instilled in people, this is precisely the reason why we wrote this down or said what we said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
