utterances.text: Your tab 16, please, Mr. Jovanovic. And if you'd be good enough to turn in it to page 19. And in the English version, if --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just be of assistance to what Mr. Jovanovic said? Mr. Jovanovic said to use the term "odvratiti," "deter," and he repeated the term that he used and that is said in the minutes and transcript. Last page, page 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the forthcoming -- oh, yes. Your Honour is absolutely right. Can -- of course we don't have to -- the one you've just been looking at was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I can get it in the index.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Exhibit 469, tab 40. The present one is 469, tab 39.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me just -- it was a correction that you were making, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to inform you that Mr. Jovanovic used the same term he used, which was "odvratiti," "to deter," and not "quell" or "calm."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true. In the English translation it says to calm or quell, whereas I said "odvratiti," meaning "deter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit, 469, tab 39 -- tab 39 but in your bundle tab 16, Mr. Jovanovic, page 19. Now, this meeting was on the 21st of January. Where were these meetings typically held? It doesn't say. Were they held at Dobranovci or Belgrade or where?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I do remember one in Belgrade and I think I attended meetings in Belgrade alone, but quite possibly I might be mistaken in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, the usual attendees including Karadzic and Mladic, Krajisnik, various other people but we haven't time to go through that in detail. On page 19 this is your contribution, Mr. Jovanovic. Starting at the second paragraph: "Therefore, the territorial link with Serbia --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Make sure the witness is following.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's your page 19, and the second paragraph, starting with the word "therefore," or starting with the concept "therefore." "The territorial link with Serbia and Montenegro, in other words with Yugoslavia, has to be ensured in an indisputable way which is not transitory. But, what is more important is to make the territory that we get nationally homogenous as soon as possible, but not by means of ethnic cleansing and so on. Ethnic cleansing are -" and the translation is "palm-offs. So we should give the peacetime process of exchange of inhabitants, in other words, migration and immigration, which will flow. What is important is that life in that future Bosnia becomes impossible Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and that everybody understands that individually, that they rush off to their original provinces. This is a strategic goal to which we should aspire, and which should be achieved. "Once this has been achieved, as the democratic party would say - 'It is ripe.' It has not been ripe for them, but it should be so for us. Everything else is then a matter of technique, including the break-up of Bosnia into three parts. "But, if they were to prevent that, then the whole idea would be brought into question. If on the contrary, freedom of movement would bring freedom of settlement and the mixing of the composition of the population to our disadvantage, then this what has been gained would gradually erode and we would basically lose everything in the future. Therefore, this should be a goal: Not to change the topic of discussion to the fact that a large number of Serbs have stayed on in foreign provinces. We should grasp the territories capable of functioning and then encourage the migration of our peoples in the direction of our provinces and others toward theirs. "How to do that, that is the thing to be wise about? But, this should be, in my opinion, our guiding thought. If this could be achieved, it could be so as soon as a couple of years time." Now, Mr. Jovanovic, I go back to my original questions. Tell us, please, candidly: The ambition was by one means or another to ensure that all Serbs lived together in a single unit. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in the translation it says that this is the break-up of Bosnia. The original says the breaking of Bosnia into three parts. So it remains as a state, but it consists of three cantons. So that's quite different. And this was done in such a way so as to deter any kind of thinking that would lead to violent solutions or something that would be violent resettlement of the population. Bosnian Serbs should be deterred from such thinking, and they should believe the laws of life that they would regulate themselves. They would do what suited the people -- what would suit the people in the Bosnia that would come, without so-called ethnic cleansing, and the population would move to the areas where they wished to live, of course pursuing an economic policy that they would --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In my original questions, of course I said nothing about violence, I said nothing about immediacy. I said was there an ultimate objective? I used a different word. You denied all of those things and denied wanting to live in a single Serb or essentially a mono-Serb state. Can you explain to the learned Judges, please -- and it's at page 19, where you say that: "Life in the future Bosnia should become impossible and that everybody has to understand they have to rush off to their original provinces, and that's a strategic goal." Can you explain that to us so we can fit it with your evidence.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what would happen in Bosnia-Herzegovina irrespective of Serbia and Montenegro. That is to say, in a future Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state, there would be these three ethnic entities or, rather, entities in accordance with agreements that would be reached, and one ethnic people would be a majority and each of them respectively. This is not a pledoyer for grabbing Bosnia and attaching it to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to -- I'm going to ask you one more question and we'll move on, but before I ask you the question, I want to -- if Mr. Nort would put page 20 on the overhead projector and the foot of page 20. Immediately, almost immediately after your contribution at this meeting with Mladic, Karadzic, and all the others there, Karadzic said this: "I think that this which Jovanovic is --" have you found it? I'm so sorry. It's about in your -- it may be 20 or it may be 21. And it's Radovan Karadzic saying: "I think this which Jovanovic is talking about." Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "I think that this which Jovanovic is talking about, has already happened to a huge extent. There was fifty-fifty of us in Zvornik. The number of inhabitants of Zvornik is now the same, approximately 50.000, and they are all Serbs. More than 24.000 Serbs from Zenica and Central Bosnia have arrived and stopped in Zvornik: If only Serbia would help us by not accepting refugees which it does not have to accept ..." Now, he was describing massive ethnic movements to achieve Serb domination of an area, wasn't he? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the position that Mr. Karadzic was presenting, and I have nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we come back to my last question to you about your own contribution in a meeting attended by all these individuals. At the foot of page 19, and it will be -- sorry, I should have checked myself. In your case it is at page 20, third paragraph, and then it's about four lines down. This is you speaking, Mr. Jovanovic: "Therefore, this should be the goal: Not to change the topic of discussion to the fact that a large number of Serbs have stayed on in foreign provinces; we should grasp the territories capable of functioning and then encourage the migration of our people in the direction of our provinces, and others towards theirs." Explain to me, please, and to the Judges how your proposition differs from what Karadzic has just described or was about to describe?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't found the exact passage. What's the page? Is it 19 or 20?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's, I think, 20, and I think it's the third paragraph, beginning "Ali ako ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a view of a peaceful development in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not violence and not by exerting physical force over other persons. This is a way of allaying the fears of the Bosnian Serbs that they would not remain a minority in their entities, that life would take its own course. And some people would go to their own entities, and other people would come to other entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So it's --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These remarks are aimed at allaying the fears of the Bosnian Serbs and that they should not worry that they would be outvoted in their own cantons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just in order to be fair to the witness, since we are now on page 20 of the Serb version of this paragraph, the interpretation that I heard here, and it's in the transcript towards the top of page 20, when he mentions ethnic cleansings, I heard Mr. Jovanovic saying ethnic cleansing should be abandoned as such, and what he said here was -- what it says in the text here is "ethnic cleansing is something that is being planted." "Ethnic cleansing is something that is being planted." That's what it says. And in the interpretation I heard that it is being given up on, as if he thought that it was a good thing and that it was being pursued and then should be given up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't see that in the transcript, but perhaps it has gone. Anyhow, thanks for the explanation, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, now that you have acknowledged that what you said in that meeting was to the effect I suggested, the position is quite simply this,

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't tell the truth when I asked you about your personal intentions right at the beginning of the questioning, did you? Because you didn't acknowledge that you had personally the desire to see ethnic migration of this kind or anything like it.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's what I'm saying now, and I never thought any such thing. It was a question of preventing ethnic cleansing and forcible transfers of population from one area to the other. And what is indicated here is to turn to life itself, life in the future and that life would take its course and determine who is going to live where. I stand by what I said, that I was always opposed to any kind of physical action against the free will of the population in any area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is that you shared an identity of interest with the Bosnian Serbs and were prepared to defend them in their actions. True or false?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was prepared to defend their right to self-determination and a free and equitable life in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What Bosnia would look like depended on them and others who lived there. I was opposed to physical action that could mean ethnic cleansing or another kind of violence that would be carried out in any part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next passage of evidence must start in private session in accordance with the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we? We should be in private now, too, for this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, from sources of information, did you, at tab 20, paragraph 7, learn of condemnation of the conduct of the Serbian side in respect of events that had then happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned about that from this dispatch, from this cable, and also from --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't identify --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, yes. So we learned from public statements condemning the conduct of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the exhibits I propose to produce, with leave of the Chamber, be given an exhibit number and then we can deal with them tab by tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 826, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And I ask that tab 20 be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 21, please, Mr. Jovanovic, and if you would be good enough, please, to look at the first page and the paragraph 1, second paragraph. Was there information about the Bosnian Serb paramilitary forces being required to cease attacks on Srebrenica and the SFRY to stop supplying Bosnian Serb paramilitary forces with weapons and military equipment? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is requested here. All I know is that President Milosevic himself attacked -- condemned attacks on Srebrenica and thought that was impermissible. As for the other issues of military nature, I really wasn't kept abreast of that. I wasn't informed about that, so I can't tell you anything specific. But I can say that we helped. We provided moral assistance and material assistance to our people in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the English version of tab 21, at page 3, at the top of that page, and in your version, Mr. Jovanovic, at the top of the second page, were the Bosnian Serbs condemned for attempting to evacuate civilians from Srebrenica and from other parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you learn information to the effect that the Bosnian Serbs were condemned for attempting to evacuate civilians from Srebrenica and from other parts of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this information, there is a mistake here where it says to evacuate civilians, because that town was not taken. It was only attacked. As I said, this attack was very severely condemned by us, by Mr. Milosevic, and that was conveyed to the leadership of Republika Srpska, and they were asked to seize it immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page -- page 3 for you, Mr. Jovanovic, and page 5 in the English. Just over halfway down the English page, and halfway down your page, Mr. Jovanovic. Second sentence of the paragraph. Did you receive information that the Serbian leadership had given assurances to the Russian officials that their army would not enter the town? Did you receive such information?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only based on this document. As for the situation on the ground, I really wasn't informed. I didn't follow that closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. You understand, Mr. Jovanovic, the questions are about the information coming to you and they're limited to that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 21, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 22, please. And of course the Chamber can see the dates as we move through, but ... Tab 22, please, Mr. Jovanovic, and it's the first page for you and it's the third paragraph for the English readers. With the proclamation of Sarajevo as a protected zone, did you learn information that the Bosnian Serbs were warned to withdraw their forces to a certain distance to avoid threatening the zone?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received that information through this document, but apart from that, I wasn't informed about other developments. I know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the shelling of Sarajevo was something that was constantly condemned by our government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 2 in the English, and I think it's the end of page 1 for you, Mr. Jovanovic. And in the English, it's the third line. Did you receive information of an official kind that ethnic cleansing and any sort of partitioning of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being condemned?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this document, we condemned it too. We condemned any kind of ethnic cleansing, and we supported the unity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not its disintegration. At the same time, we worked with other international representatives on constitutional principles for creating Bosnia as a confederation or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- another form of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 22, if you please. Tab 24 comes next. Tab 23 is void. Tab 24, the Chamber will observe the details at the top. The distribution list is similar. This is information coming to you from elsewhere, but it was information about the key significance -- sorry, it's page 1 of the English, the first substantive paragraph; and it's in the Serbian, likewise the first substantive paragraph. Did you receive information about the symbolic significance of Sarajevo being of the essence to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Without it, its identity or its sovereignty being lost?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned, based on this document and also based on the discussions we had with international representatives. At the same time, this was our position. We were constantly opposed to the shelling. In Dayton, Mr. Milosevic put this into practice by saying that the entire Sarajevo ought to belong to Bosniaks, to the Muslim part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to divert from the particular topics of the documents just for one or two questions because they come at the right sequence. Who was paying for the Bosnian Serb army, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I did not deal with military issues in any way, nor was I informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were a foreign minister. You were later the representative at the United Nations. You obviously followed this trial. You've spoken extensively about this Tribunal, and we may have time to look at that. Are you telling the Chamber that you have no idea whether Serbia assisted financially with the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we provided material including financial assistance to the Bosnian Serbs in all aspects of their lives. Now, as for the salaries of officers, I don't know about that specifically. I heard that that was the case. I heard it not only at this trial but in other places as well, although I have no information myself about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first hear about it then?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that long ago. I didn't know about that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what I want you to help us with is this: If there was such condemnation of the attack on Sarajevo, why wasn't the supply line of money and offices simply cut off by this accused? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We as the parent state could not abandon our people to their fate. We could not allow them to die of hunger. This is something similar to what Croatia did with respect to Herceg-Bosna. Therefore, to cut the assistance would have been inhumane. However, on the 4th of August, 1994, we did something similar to that, although the ban did not apply to assistance in terms of food, medication, and clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does your last answer mean that you understood and knew at the time that the Bosnian Serbs were getting military assistance in the form of officers, money, and armaments? Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any firsthand information about that. All I had were things I heard from other people about financial assistance. I did not have any other information, nor was any information to that effect provided to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept -- you see, you told us that the accused condemned the years of attack on Srebrenica. You speak of humane assistance. What about the humane problems of the thousands of Muslims who were killed in Srebrenica? Can you help us with why support wasn't cut off when it could have been?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you refer to the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, or perhaps you're referring to the attacks on Srebrenica in 1993, I'm not quite sure. If you're referring to Srebrenica in 1995, then that was an atrocious massacre. As far as 1993, as far as I know, Srebrenica did not fall then. It was only under attacks. And naturally, in the course of those attacks there were casualties on both sides. President Milosevic, the governments, both the federal and republican governments condemned attacks on those protected areas. I have to say that the protected areas were never clear as a concept, and they were never really demilitarised. First in Srebrenica, because there were cases there that Muslim soldiers stormed Serb villages and committed grave crimes there. Therefore, the concept of protected areas wasn't clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're past the time for the break. I should say that the tabs and the index are to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. And I think -- had I already produced tab 22? If not, may I do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 24. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, when we broke, I think you were seeking the admission of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- tab 24. The Court deputy wasn't certain about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you to Your Honour and the Court deputy. Your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Honour, I'm going to miss tab 25. It's a document we've looked at with another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 26, please, Mr. Jovanovic, and it's a short document for you to look at. It's the first paragraph in each version. Did you receive information about 120-millimetre projectiles being fired on Sarajevo from Bosnian Serb positions, followed by UN overflights?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I was not kept abreast of information of that nature, of military nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honours will perhaps be good enough to look at the second page, document in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the witness would be good enough to look at the second page of his. Thinking back, please, Mr. Jovanovic. This information came to you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did, but I'm afraid that at the time, I was not in the country. I had a long tour of African countries. But even had I been present, had this information reached me, this would not have changed anything because this was just one of numerous informations -- information that came in from various sources discussing the situation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can confirm that this information came into the Foreign Ministry and was available to the government? Yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, if this is marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 26 -- tab 26.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we lay on the overhead projector briefly tab 27. Your Honours, just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document is -- the document on the overhead projector we see goes back, and it has its relevance really now. This is dated the 16th of April of 1993, and it's a Resolution of the Security Council. Do you recall this Resolution, please, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say precisely, because this was 15 years ago and there were many such Resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Security Council followed very closely the situation and adopted various documents about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is what we see here under the heading "Taking note," is that "the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro should immediately in pursuance of its undertaking take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of the crime of genocide." Do you remember that extraordinarily strong decision being taken in respect of your country? As foreign minister, you must have been aware of it.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly I was familiar with this dispatch, although I can't remember when it was adopted exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And under the heading "Concerned," do you see a reference to "concerned by the pattern of hostilities by Bosnian Serb paramilitary units"? Do you remember that concern being expressed?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, concern was frequently expressed, not only on that occasion. That became quite a regular practice, to mention these forces in such documents and to condemn their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before I return to the sequence of information material that we've been covering, just tell me this: As foreign minister for Serbia or of the Federal Republic of Serbia and Montenegro or Yugoslavia, there could be no justification in 1991, could there, for the accused to establish paramilitary forces himself? Could there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with any paramilitary forces established that year in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of forces that came to be known as the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with them, but I have to say that it was not until my return from New York that I became familiar with their names. Prior to that, I did not follow their activities, nor did I know them under that title. As far as I know, they were created much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is going to be a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide. If paramilitary forces were established by this accused in 1991 and used outside Serbia and Montenegro, were you ever informed of that, you as a member of the government?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, these forces were not established in 1991 but later, in 1996 or around that time. On the other hand, I've already said that I was not kept informed about any military issues, nor did I follow those issues closely. I know for a fact that there were no paramilitary formations in Serbia in 1991 except those belonging to various political parties, and those formations acted under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me, as foreign -- looking back at the screen and seeing that in April 1993 the United Nations reaffirmed -- under "Reaffirming the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," you as foreign minister, does that mean that you owed duties in relation to this sovereign state in your capacity as a foreign minister?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. And we confirmed that through documents and early statements and also in all of our contacts with international intermediaries. We confirmed that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ought to be constitutionally structured as an independent state, and we never challenged that identity or independence of that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Jovanovic. Should you, as a foreign minister with those duties, have been informed of the military activity, if any, of Serbia through paramilitaries or otherwise on that foreign state? Should you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were such activities. I don't think there were, because Serbia was not a party to a war, nor did it send its army --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us you're a life-long diplomat. You've been a politician for several years as well. Please tell the Chamber: If one state sends military forces to another state, is that something of which the foreign minister and the Foreign Ministry needs to be aware? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that Serbia sent its army or parts of its army to another state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I have barely time to wait for the answers. We'll move on -- if they're not going to be given. We'll move on, please, to tab 28. And again, did you receive information -- second paragraph on the first page of each version. Did you receive concern expressed about the prevention of the formal functioning of Sarajevo airport, the suspension of humanitarian aid, a result of efforts by Bosnian Serbs? Did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably received it if I was in Belgrade at the time, but let me stress once again, because of the interruption of all economic and political relations with Serbia and Yugoslavia at that time, we didn't have any contacts, and we weren't able to exert any serious influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 29 I don't have time to deal with in detail. I may, I suppose, come back to it. Just help us: On the 5th of May, 1995, where were you? You tell us you were out of the country at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. Well, I was during the summer absent during the summer. I can't from this point in time remember where I actually was. I might have been in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Speaking to the accused by telephone from time to time?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, and not that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May tab 28 be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 30, please. Did you receive information - and the Chamber will notice the dates - did you receive information, tab 28, first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 30, Your Honours. My mistake. Tab 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive information about condemnation of the Bosnian Serbs about an attack over the protected zone?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me, then certainly I did, because I was mentioned here, and I repeat that our position was that the protected areas must not be attacked, nor must they be used for --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Jovanovic. Page 2 of 3 for the English readers, and page 2 for you, Mr. Jovanovic, paragraph 3. Did you receive information that Great Britain was asking the Serbs to stop shelling activities, welcoming the efforts invested by this accused and General Smith?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that's how it was, as it says here, but from this point in time, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May tab 30 please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 31, please, Mr. Jovanovic. Did you receive information - there's a single paragraph here - that Sarajevo had been deprived for many months of supply and there was a fear of unpredictable consequences and of armed conflict with the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that I was, and I certainly was, although once again I probably wasn't there, but that's not important. And I'd like to stress again that at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we had cut off relations with --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Tab 32. The Chamber will observe a different location and will have the date in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do we have a translation of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if Your Honours haven't received it. Yes, we do. It's with your staff, I think. It's one of the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Slightly different appearance. I suppose different translation staff dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At tab 32, different source of information. Were you aware that a potentially friendly source was -- this is the second bullet point, fourth line, in both cases on the first page. Were you aware that a friendly source was -- well, friendly contact was pressing you to convince Pale to give up the blockade of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly, but probably that was it. A lot of time has gone by, of course, but let me stress once again that we always condemned the siege of Sarajevo, and we always did our best to help to open the corridor for humanitarian aid and other assistance but we had no contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May tab 31 and 32 be produced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have we dealt with tab 30? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 33. And the Chamber will note the date. Did you receive information about Bosnian Serbs opening tank fire on Srebrenica, the loss of life and with wounded, and shelling Srebrenica and the 8th and 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just on the basis of this document, but some personal knowledge, no, we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will, if you turn to page 3 at the foot, see -- and then on page 4, see matters of obvious interest. I won't deal with it in open session. May tab 33 be produced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 34. There is now, of course, a flurry of activity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what Mr. Nice wants the witness to answer with respect to all these tabs. All he is doing is including and tendering documents which, according to their contents, he doesn't use them as raising questions and doesn't allow for the witness to answer. This is just routine information which in my opinion have no value at all for what he is trying to prove, no probative value at all. Without going into the contents, all he can do is tender them as part of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the accused wishes to admit all these exhibits, all the code cables as documents of information coming to this witness and also to the accused, I'm only too content to use my limited time for another purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think what he's seeking to do is to utilise the witness's information, information that was available to the witness by virtue of his official position to confirm as a matter of fact information in the tabs, and then it becomes evidence. Mr. Nice also indicated that if you weren't challenging the information in the documents, then he would be -- he could expedite the proceedings appreciably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I make it plain, I'm always happy to discuss matters with the accused or with his representatives at any time they want to, and if the accused would like me, in general terms, to seek admissions with his associates, I'm only too delighted to do so but I understand that such communication has been effectively -- for these purposes has been effectively ruled out. Sometimes, Your Honours, one is able to say that silence assent, but I fear on this occasion it may not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, of course we cannot say that certain information is not being challenged because in one of these tabs, for instance, it is said and claimed that Yugoslavia should cease to assist paramilitary formations of the Bosnian Serbs. Yugoslavia never helped anybody's paramilitary formations. So Yugoslavia did and Serbia did help Republika Srpska and the army of Republika Srpska, but never paramilitary formations. Therefore, there are things to be challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is a matter that you could raise in re-examination. Was that specifically put to the witness, that question, the question of assistance --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's only the information that was coming and I can't remember now if that's one of the bits I've read out or not. Yes. That -- that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Nice, all that's happening here is you are identifying what material was brought to the attention of this witness and hence the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And whether or not it's accurate is plainly, in many instances, a matter in dispute, and it makes no difference to the status of that dispute if the accused was simply to acknowledge that these documents were brought to his attention, and that's all that you are doing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. It's going to serve an additional function in relation to a question I ask of this witness, but on the principle problem, as I explained in my preparatory remarks, yes. So it's up to him if he wants to admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you expect me to say? Well, these documents are being tendered by Mr. Nice, not myself. As far as I'm concerned, these are routine informations, hundreds of like coming in every day. So I don't see any importance in them for what Mr. Nice is trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Milosevic, if you were simply to acknowledge that that was the case and accept it, then we could spend time Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the witness - as could you - spend more time with the witness exploring the facts that lie behind them or within the documents. But because of the way courts work, it's necessary for this exercise to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid the accused's attitude is as it is, and for the avoidance of any doubt so he can understand the position, it will be our case in due course that this is the very best level of information of this type, whether reliable or not, being, of course, for others to decide. I think I'm up to tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, if you could look at that, please. Did you receive in tab 34 information, paragraph 1, that the Bosnian Serbs were being asked to stop their offensive, the date will be before the Court, and to withdraw from Srebrenica? And if you turn to page 2 in the --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 34, page 1, paragraph 1, line 2.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on page 2 at -- and in --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the Bosnian -- in the Serbian, I beg your pardon, on the -- I think the bottom of the first page, or of the second page. Did you receive information about the threat to execute 30 Dutch soldiers, and after the Serb --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We couldn't learn that -- receive that information from anyone because we didn't have any contacts with the leadership of Republika Srpska, neither did we in any way control the development of the situation there at all. But from this tab, we can see that it is addressed to me, so we could only learn about it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me, at this time, where were you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but quite possibly I was absent, because usually I would travel during the summer. But I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is an absolutely critical time for the history of this war. Think back, please, and you tell us where you were.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't remember exactly, because I visited many countries during the summer in 1993, 1994, and 1995. So quite simply I can't remember. I could if I had some documents to remind me from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help me with this: The events that are being covered in these cables are events of the gravest kind. You're a government minister. When did you first discuss them with the accused, these events?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we learnt through the press that Srebrenica had fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Through the press --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a surprise, and of course we didn't condone it, but we didn't have the possibility of talking about that with the leadership of Republika Srpska. So I can't tell you more than that. I wasn't kept informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... learn of it through the press, please, that Srebrenica had fallen?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say exactly. Probably several days, depending on what the press reported. I don't think a lot of time went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you learnt about it, did you have a face-to-face meeting with the accused? Pretty important matter. Did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him whether in connection with that or in connection with other matters. I know that he was very surprised and that he was very angry. His reaction was one of anger. Not only because it was a protected area which had to be respected, but also because the army of Republika Srpska did it of its own bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did he tell you about his telephone conversations with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't discuss that at all. It never came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he say anything about efforts that he made to dissuade Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we discussed that. Possibly he did try to dissuade Mladic but I don't know about it because we didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Give us an idea of the government of which you were a part and the seniority of members. In some governments the foreign minister's pretty near to being the second to top dog, the second most important person. In your government where did you, as foreign minister, rank? Pretty important?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that for myself. No minister can. No minister can say he was important, but he did his best to be important through his contribution. And I was directly responsible to the Prime Minister Kontic, and I had contacts with the president of Yugoslavia as well, and President Milosevic at that time was the President of Serbia. So I wasn't his immediate second, the second man. But of course we did meet and exchange views on certain matters and on some situations that were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Tab 35, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 34, may it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We come to tab 35, already go on the -- no. Rapidly on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware contemporaneously by our Exhibit 547, tab 33, that on the 12th of July the United Nations Security Council condemned the offensive by Bosnian Serb forces against Srebrenica and, in particular, the detention of Bosnian Serb forces -- by Bosnian Serb forces of UNPROFOR personnel? Were you aware of that on the same day, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If not that day, then probably the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this paper arrived with some delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 36, please. This is -- if you look at tab 36, this comes from a different source. And did you learn information - and it's differently presented so we have the advantage of paragraph numbers - that a man called Pejanovic -- now, you know Pejanovic, don't you? You know who he is. You'll see him at the end of the paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him once in Geneva. He was a member of the delegation of Bosnian Muslims, but we didn't talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't understand or, rather, I can't find my way around these paragraphs. Is he -- is Mr. Nice talking about tab 36? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm talking about tab 36. And if the accused goes to the foot of the first page, he'll see as part of the paragraph 2, "Zbog aktuelnosti prvi blok."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is Pejanovic a Bosnian Muslim or a Bosnian Serb?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, he was one of those unusual Serbs who pressed not the Serb cause but the multi-ethnic cause in Bosnia, didn't he? He wasn't interested in separation. He was interested in continued integration of all the ethnic groups; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he wanted to be. I know that he was one of the Serbs that remained in the Presidency led by Mr. Izetbegovic and that he was very consistent and fervent in supporting his policy and stands in respect of the Bosnian crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a man who we can see on page -- English page 2 and, as I say, at the foot of page 1 for you. This is a man of a different thought pattern from the SPS, who presented -- who said that things were happening that were the last moment to wake up -- I beg your pardon. The last moment to wake up the conscience of mankind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SPS is the abbreviation for the Socialist Party of Serbia. I see nowhere here any mention of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What paragraph is this, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not mentioned at all. I mentioned SPS. I should have said SBS. SDS. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's get back to the point, Mr. Jovanovic. Here you received information on the date given from this man that it was the last moment to wake up the conscience of mankind. If we go to paragraph 3, line 3, we see an estimation of what he proposed.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yep. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is that our position was full support to the plan of the Contact Group and condemnation of all furtherance of war in any of its shapes or forms, and that we repeated this for a year prior to that, so that no hostilities in Bosnia or any armed conflict can be ascribed to our intentions, because we were against hostilities as a whole and asked that they be stopped in all directions and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours will also see paragraph 4 at the foot of page 2. Too much detail maybe for open session, but I ask that this document be admitted. It's clear that it arrived. Tab 36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 37, please, Mr. Jovanovic, a shorter document from a different source. Its date will be noted. Now, then, you've told us that you learnt about the fall of Srebrenica from the newspapers. Take your time, please. Look at the document. Look at the second page of the document, and tell the Court on which day information must have come to you and to this accused about the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. It is the first information that reached us, and for us it was astounding. We were terribly surprised, and we didn't expect this move on the part of Republika Srpska with respect to that particular town. And we learnt about it when the information reached us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have private session for just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, you and this accused were aware of the fall of Srebrenica not later than the 13th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's roughly how it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Roughly or certainly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the reference be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Redact that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 37, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move on, then, to tab 38. On this occasion, a slightly longer document. If we look simply at the page 1. Did you become aware, line 3 of the first substantive paragraph, that emphasis was being placed on the request that Bosnian Serbs should stop their offensive and withdraw from Srebrenica as well as to liberate unconditionally UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned that from this document that arrived. We heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that such a request had been formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 38, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 39, Mr. Jovanovic. Different source, different --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused is raising matters that shouldn't be raised in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to redact that -- those references.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And second, these interventions of his, which are not single, have the effect, if not the purpose, of taking time; and third if he wants to admit the material, I'm still open to that admission. But otherwise, I must press on and get to the end of this exercise, which won't take very much longer, but it will, I'm afraid, take a bit of time. Can we go to tab 39, please, if 38 has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 39. 39. Did you receive information about the Bosnian Serbs, third line, firing 22 missiles towards Potocari where Dutch troops and refugees were located, and an estimation of 25 or 27.000 refugees, matters of that sort, heading towards the direction of Tuzla. Did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that I received it. It says so in the heading and it's probably correct. Or, rather, that it was sent to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May that be admitted, please? Tab 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 40. The Court will see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive information -- on the second substantive paragraph, did you receive information on the condemnation of the activity of the Bosnian Serbs? And at page 2 in the English and at page 2 in your version, Mr. Jovanovic, in the middle of the page, did you receive information that a sometimes friendly country, or thought to be a friendly country said that the occupation of Srebrenica started a new phase in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had the opportunity of reading this document so that I could follow exactly what you know from your own reading, but it is indicated here that I am one of the recipients, so I assume that it had reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And also on the same page, did you receive information which the Court can see at the foot of page 2, did you receive information about the attitude of Russia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we received this document, then we had to receive everything Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that this document contains, including that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 40, if the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 41, please, Mr. Jovanovic. From another source. Did you receive information about the extension of Serb aggression on the civil population of Srebrenica? With reference to public media broadcasts of the suffering of civilians and reference to the helplessness of the Dutch Blue Berets.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here -- I mean, my name is also written down here. That means that it reached me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Come on, think back, Mr. Jovanovic. We are dealing with the most grave alleged crime since the Second World War, and I want you to tell this Court if you, foreign minister of one of the countries said to have been involved, received information about it. Are you going to retreat to saying, "If it's in the document, then I must have done," or are you going to tell us what your active memory was -- is?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know anything more about this tragic event than what the newspapers said and what arrived in this way. Of course these were shocking news, but I always had to take them with a grain of salt before receiving authentic information that that was correct, before I received another type of confirmation. No confirmation arrived, at least not while I was minister. So this entire situation regarding Srebrenica was in the dark, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've only taken a sentence or so from each of these documents but you've had a chance to see them and you can have a look at them probably over the weekend. They contain a lot of information. What more did you want? And why was it necessary to take a grain or might it have been a kilogramme of salt with them? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Bosnian Serbs, although they were condemned from many quarters, often rightly so, they were also being blamed for things that they were not guilty of. As Vaso Miskin, Markale 1, Markale 2, and this attack against them concerning Srebrenica is something that I personally had to receive with shock, of course, but then on the other hand I wanted to get some kind of confirmation that that is exactly what happened, that it wasn't a kind of campaign again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ring up Mladic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why not? You tell us that you wanted to know the truth. What efforts did you make to find out? Thousands of people died at Srebrenica, Mr. Jovanovic. You were the foreign minister. What efforts did you make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To do what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To find out what had happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I did not have any telephone or other contacts with General Mladic except that I saw him a few times at some meetings that he had been invited to. For the most part it was meetings with international intermediaries but we never talked about the situation there. I was not an interlocutor of his and I did not have enough knowledge to discuss such matters. On the other hand, I was waiting for the matter to be clarified, to be confirmed from several source so that I could take it as an indisputable fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm afraid I will have to detain the witness until next week, obviously, but in order to just see where we've got, where we eventually get to with the witness and to use the next ten minutes in a slightly different way, I wonder if the Chamber would be good enough to go to tab 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I wonder if you, Mr. Jovanovic, would go to tab 55 as well. In light of your protestations about how concerned you were and what efforts you made, and we'll come back and have a look at the rest of the information coming to you. Sorry, tab 55. My mistake. I should have taken you first of all to tab 52. Now, tab 52, which can go on the overhead projector, if you've got a copy, comes a little bit later. It comes in November of 1995. And it's a document that you sent, a letter that you sent as by then the charges d'affaires of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: See what it says. Next page, please, Mr. Nort. You said this: "The claims that the Yugoslav army had either directly or indirectly taken part in the operation for the liberation of the Muslim military stronghold of Srebrenica in July 1995 are completely unfounded. "Such falsehoods, as well as untrue allegations of the existence of prison camps for the Muslims in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, are part of well-known campaigns always launched at crucial moments when peace in the war-torn regions of the previous Yugoslavia is about to be reached. "... It is obvious -- on this occasion it is obvious that what is at stake is an attempt to exert pressure on the Serb side during the peace process and negotiations in Dayton since not a single member of the Yugoslav army participated in the battles around Srebrenica and there are no camps for Muslim prisoners ..." Next paragraph. We come back to what you've already been telling us about. "Yugoslavia urges and supports the investigation of war crimes ..." Next sentence: "The latest campaign by Western media, which accuses only the Serbs without any proof does not contribute to this goal, whose aim is a propaganda war which is hardly a necessary element for conducting peace talks in Dayton." And then you wrote this: "Lacking an opportunity to orchestrate a third Markale incident, the forces that obviously do not seek peace are spreading this disinformation in order to divert the attention of the world public from Yugoslavia's constructive and peaceful policy, thus diminishing the prospects of a positive outcome ..." Is that still your view?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my view. That is the view of the federal government that sent this statement, along with instructions that it be forwarded to the president of the Security Council and to have it circulated as a Security Council document, and I carried that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then just one point on this one before we turn to the next document, which I will just get done in time. First paragraph, second line. What's this liberation about? Who is being liberated? Twenty or 30.000 Muslims who were driven out or killed? Who is being liberated?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not my paper. It's paper of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any idea who --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it's a question of expression. It would have been more precise to say "the taking of Srebrenica," not "the liberation of Srebrenica," because there were -- there were, though, a great many Serbs there, not only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where can you find those words?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First paragraph. First paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we please -- and may that tab 52 as well as the original -- tab 41 I've missed, tab 41 and 52. Can I take you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I take you in the remaining five minutes, if I have five minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To tab 55. Tab 55, please, Mr. Jovanovic. And I provided you with it overnight. I kept nothing back from you. And this is a letter you wrote on the 18th of December. And we'll just look at two parts of it. It's a letter that you wrote to the United Nations, and on the first page -- no, next page, please, Mr. Nort. Foot of the first page. Foot of that page. Push it up. Thank you. Up. Right. Thank you very much. "I would like to draw your attention to the following facts which are based on the reports provided by the official authorities of the Republika Srpska. These reports, which may be verified, strongly contradict the above allegations and are intended to shed new light on the events in question." Next page, please, Mr. Nort. I don't have time to do paragraph 1, A, B, C, D and E, but let's look at paragraph 2. "Immediately before the takeover of Srebrenica by the army of the Republika Srpska, disorders and conflicts within the Bosnian Muslim army in that enclave erupted. In the clashes that ensued, those units that wanted to continue fighting were mercilessly killing those who wanted to surrender and were favour of cease-fire. Since the units of the army of Republika Srpska did not have access to those areas at that time, it was only after the fall of the enclave that the bodies of Muslim fighters and civilians who died as a result of the infighting were discovered. This situation was abused by the Bosnian Muslim government to further its propaganda campaign of the alleged mass killings and disappearance of Muslims from the area." Mr. Jovanovic, you know of the admissions that have been made by the Republika Srpska publicly in recent months about 7.000 dead. Now, can you help us, please, with how you came to write that paragraph, blaming the Muslims for their own deaths? Because just to remind you, this isn't a letter that comes from the government; this comes from you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain straight away? This is an omission, an omission on my part, because this document was not intended for the Security Council at all. It was intended for head of the Russian mission who, it so happened, was then president of the Security Council as well. The point was that he knew that soon a Security Council session would be held precisely dedicated to Srebrenica, and he asked us to give him any kind of information about what had happened there. I asked my Foreign Ministry for this information, and after a long time and after a lot of insistence, instead of information, I got the information that the leadership of Republika Srpska had sent. It was a rather long text. Then at the senior staff meeting of our mission, I told my deputy chief of mission to translate those parts that seemed logical to him and to send them, of course with my signature, to the head of the Russian mission so that, if he wished, he could use some of it in his speech there. However, my deputy chief of mission misunderstood this, that he was not supposed to send it to him in his capacity as president of the Security Council but rather in his capacity as head of the Russian mission. I signed this hastily because I didn't have time to check out before that whether he had done this properly. Proof of this can be found with all the members of the staff of the mission then. The following day everybody realised what happened. My omission was obvious and I was wondering after that what to do, whether to withdraw this or to let things go as they were. Unfortunately, this had already been circulated, it had produced a certain effect, and in this vacillation as to what I was supposed to do, I let things go along the way they did, and I'm sorry about the omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My last question for today, with His Honour's leave, is this: I don't accept, on behalf of the Prosecution, your account of writing a letter like this by accident. You remember I asked you earlier whether you and the Bosnian Serbs had an identity of interest? I'd like you to think about that question again, because my suggestion to you is that you plainly did. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I do not accept that I did this with intent. There were four people who were with me then who can confirm that it was a mistake. If you wish, I can give you their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I haven't been able to finish today. I had very much hoped to. Had it been possible to put in the documents by admission, I might have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will have to adjourn now and we'll have to resume next Tuesday at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.44 p.m.,
